title: RSA-1999-1-001 — Fedsure Life Assurance Ltd and Others v. Greater Johannesburg Transitional Metropolitan Council and Others
text:
The lawfulness of the resolution increasing property rates within the Eastern Metropolitan Substructure (the EMS), whose additional funds were necessary, not for the EMS's own purposes, but rather for the payment of a levy to the Greater Johannesburg Transitional Metropolitan Council (the TMC). Budget involves making considered estimates and certain contingent liabilities and such expenditures do not undermine the validity of the property rates imposed.

The levy imposed by the TMC on the EMS and Northern Metropolitan Substructure (the NMS) is to be equitable and based on the gross or rates income of the substructures.

The imposed levy must be necessary for the TMC to exercise its powers and perform its functions and must be based on a uniform structure for the TMC's area of jurisdiction.

The appellants, ten corporate ratepayers in the EMS, objected to a substantial increase in their property rates. They challenged the lawfulness of certain resolutions adopted by the TMC and the EMS in relation to their respective 1996/97 budgets which had given rise to the increase in property rates. The budgets were drawn up in accordance with a policy negotiated and agreed to by the TMC and its four substructures. At the heart of this policy were two principles: (1) that a uniform rate should be imposed on land and rights in land across the greater Johannesburg region and (2) that the combined budgets of the individual bodies should balance. Calculations revealed that if a general rate of 6.45 cents in the Rand was charged on land and rights in land within the greater Johannesburg area, total income would meet total expenditure. Therefore, by means of the challenged resolutions, surpluses generated in the EMS and NMS were paid as levies to the TMC. The TMC retained funds sufficient to balance its own budget and paid the remainder to the Western Metropolitan Substructure (the WMS) and the Southern Metropolitan Substructure (the SMS) in the form of subsidies.

The initial application was brought to the Witwatersrand High Court to have the rates, levies and subsidies set aside. The High Court found, per Goldstein J, that the resolutions were lawful and dismissed the application.

The appellants first appealed to the Supreme Court of Appeal (the SCA) against the finding of the Witwatersrand High Court. The SCA found that it was not able to entertain the appeal since the attacks raised constitutional issues and the interim Constitution vests such jurisdiction, not in the SCA, but in the Constitutional Court. Accordingly it referred two questions to the Constitutional Court: (1) whether the resolutions were consistent with the interim Constitution and (2) if they were, whether the SCA had any residual power to decide the various challenges.

The resolutions were challenged on a series of grounds. At the hearing in the SCA, the parties agreed that the resolutions relating to the rates, levies and subsidies were "administrative actions" as contemplated in Section 24 of the interim Constitution. In the Constitutional Court, however, the respondents argued that they were legislative and not administrative actions. The court accepted this argument, but the justices agreed that all legislation must comply with the Constitution and the important principle of the Constitution, that is, the rule of law, which means at the very least that any exercise of power by an organ of State must fall within the limits of the power conferred on that body. Courts, including the Constitutional Court, may thus review and set aside legislative action which does not comply with this principle of "legality".

Four challenges were mounted by the appellants against the EMS's and the TMC's resolutions respectively. However, only three are relevant for the purpose of the present exercise.

The first challenge by the appellants was that the resolution increasing property rates within the EMS was unlawful since these additional funds were necessary, not for the EMS's own purposes, but rather for the payment of a levy to the TMC. The Constitutional Court unanimously rejected this challenge on the basis that the process of drawing up a budget involves making considered estimates as to items of expenditure which are likely to be incurred during the relevant financial year. In the ordinary course of events, certain contingent liabilities will not materialise, or will place a lesser or greater drain on resources than originally anticipated. Such outcome cannot be said to entitle ratepayers to challenge the validity of the budget itself. It was held further that, even if the TMC levy was unlawful, the fact that the EMS provided in its budget for such expenditure did not undermine the validity of the property rates imposed by the EMS.

The second challenge was that the resolution of the TMC imposing a levy on the EMS and NMS was unlawful because the levy was not equitable and was not based on the gross or rates income of the substructures as required by Item 23.a of Annexure A to the Premiers Proclamation 35 of 1995 (Gauteng Province). The court was evenly divided on this question.

In a joint judgment of Chaskalson P, Goldstone J and O'Regan J, concurred in by Ackermann J and Madala J, it was held that the levy was not sufficiently closely linked to either gross or rates income for it to have been "based on" such income. It was found that the evidence indicated that the levy was based on the surpluses generated in the EMS and NMS. Therefore, it was held that the TMC levy was unlawful. This finding rendered it unnecessary for these justices to express any opinion on the appellants' third challenge.

In a separate judgment by Kriegler J, concurred in by Langa DP, Mokgoro J, Sachs J and Yacoob J, it was found that it was not necessary that the levy be based exclusively on gross income. It was sufficient that the levy be related to gross income. Therefore, it was held that the levy was directly related to the EMS's gross income and thus that the TMC levy was lawful.

The third challenge was that the levy was unlawful on the basis that it was not necessary for the TMC to exercise its powers and perform its functions and that it was not based on a uniform structure for the TMC's area of jurisdiction as required by Section 178.2 of the interim Constitution. Only Kriegler J's finding in relation to the second challenge rendered it necessary to consider this third attack. Kriegler J observed that the interdependence of the TMC and its four substructures, and the TMC's constitutional duty to provide for the well-being of all persons within its area of jurisdiction, entailed that it had the power to impose a levy on one substructure for the purpose, not only of balancing its own budget, but also of making a grant to subsidise another substructure's deficit. Given the co-operation between the TMC and its substructures in financing each other's expenditure, and in particular the decisions to standardise property rate and service tariffs across the greater Johannesburg region, the levy was based on a uniform structure for the TMC's area of jurisdiction. Therefore, Kriegler J held that the TMC levy was lawful.

In relation to the second of the questions referred by the SCA, the justices were agreed that the SCA did not have jurisdiction under the interim Constitution to decide any matter which the Constitutional Court was empowered to decide. In the opinion of the Constitutional Court, this scheme was undesirable. It introduced uncertainty as to which court should hear particular cases and deprived the Constitutional Court of the views of the SCA on constitutional issues. The 1996 Constitution removed this jurisdictional bar by allowing the SCA to hear constitutional cases. It was therefore held that in future cases falling under the interim Constitution, it would be in the interest of justice for the SCA to exercise the jurisdiction conferred on it by the 1996 Constitution. However, it should decide the case in terms of the law in force at the time that the relevant cause of action arose.

As the justices were evenly divided, however, on the lawfulness of the TMC levy imposed on the EMS, there was no clear majority in favour of reversing the finding of Witwatersrand High Court. The appeal on this issue therefore also had to fail. Accordingly the entire appeal was dismissed.
